md_streamside.blurb: Streamside is the main bouldering circuit at Morgan Run, a wooded natural area in Carroll County. The problems sit on schist blocks scattered along a creek, with trails that mostly follow the water, so finding your way around is easy and the farthest boulders are only a short walk from the car. Nearly everything here is a boulder problem, with a broad spread: plenty of V0 to V3, a solid middle, and a handful of hard V6 to V8 lines. The stone can be sharp on the skin, and summer brings heavy foliage, ticks and sticky heat, so cooler months are the more comfortable time to visit.
md_streamside.parking_note: A small lot sits on Klee Mill Road just past the bridge, at the foot of the dip. The Streamside boulders are on the same side of the road as the lot.
md_streamside.approach: Trails run along the creek from the lot; the most distant boulders are about five minutes away.

md_long_wall.blurb: Long Wall is one of the taller bouldering walls in the Northwest Branch stream valley near Silver Spring, tucked downstream from the first boulders you meet on the trail. Expect crystalline gneiss with incut holds that can be sharp on the fingers and good footholds. The problems skew friendly, with most in the V0 to V3 range and a few hard ones near the top end, but the height means landings and spotting deserve attention; some climbers bring a rope for the taller lines. It can be hard to find on a first visit, so allow extra time to walk the stream path.

md_jonah_boulder.blurb: Jonah Boulder is one of the bigger blocks along the Cliff Trail in Cunningham Falls State Park, in the Catoctin Mountains. The problems here lean hard: most fall in the V4 to V7 range, with a couple at V8 and only a few easier warm-ups. The boulders stand among the woods and outcrops beside a steep, rocky trail that climbs toward the falls. Brush your holds and clean tick marks when you leave, since this is a popular park with a lot of foot traffic.
md_jonah_boulder.parking_note: Leave the car in the William Houck area near Hunting Creek Lake, where the Cliff Trail begins.
md_jonah_boulder.approach: Follow the yellow-blazed Cliff Trail uphill a few hundred feet to a clearing holding several large boulders; Jonah is among them.

md_woodstock_rock.blurb: Woodstock Rock is a compact gneiss crag of roughly 40 feet in Patapsco Valley State Park, known for steep, tiered overhangs with blocky jugs. It is more powerful than the other Patapsco crags: it is hard to find a line without an overhang, and a cave on the left offers long roof problems. Most people top-rope or boulder, with a smaller number of gear leads and no bolted lines. The face stays shaded and faces north, so it suits late spring through early fall, but seepage from the cracks keeps it wet for a couple of days after heavy rain.
md_woodstock_rock.parking_note: Use the large gravel lot opposite the Woodstock Inn on Woodstock Road; it is shared with anglers, hikers and riders.
md_woodstock_rock.approach: A trail starts at the back of the lot and reaches the base after roughly 800 feet.

md_white_rocks.blurb: White Rocks is the remote cliff on Sugarloaf Mountain, a quartzite monadnock rising above the Maryland countryside. The rock is secure but sharp, so hands and ropes take a beating. Climbing is mostly trad and top-rope on a vertical face that asks a bit more of the leader than the busier main crags, plus boulders on the slope below. There is a feeling of exposure at the top and a fine view. Wind can be strong, especially in colder months, and the walk in is long enough that crowds are thinner than near the main parking area.

ma_red_rock_main_area.blurb: Red Rock Main Area is the principal cliff at Redrocks on Cape Ann, a reddish granite face a short walk off the trail near Gloucester. Most of the climbing is on gear or sport bolts, with some top-roping that needs long slings to reach anchors. Routes span easy slabs at the north end up to hard modern lines, though the bulk fall between 5.8 and 5.11. Several lines are long for greater Boston, and a boulder sits at the south end of the face. Land ownership around the cliff is murky, so keep a low profile and leave no trace.

ma_nira_rock.blurb: Nira Rock is a small urban outcrop of puddingstone in Boston's Jamaica Plain, in a former quarry with an upper and lower section. The conglomerate has varied textures, and the climbing is mainly bouldering, from VB through the V8 range, plus a few top-rope lines and one bolted face route. It is a quick after-work spot reachable by transit. Because it is a city park, watch for broken glass around the base, and expect the occasional pebble to pop out of the holds.
ma_nira_rock.parking_note: Cars can go at the dead end of Grotto Glen Road or along Nira Avenue. The Green Line to Heath Street also works for a walk-in.

ma_main_crag.blurb: Main Crag is the long band of granite that holds most of the climbing at College Rock in Hopkinton. Routes are short, about 12 to 35 feet, and mostly set up for top-rope, with some gear leads and a couple of boulder problems. Grades run from very easy to 5.11, and most sit between 5.7 and 5.10. The climbing is technical and sequential, and the grades can feel stiff. Shaded woods keep the rock cool and slow to dry after rain, and the dirt lot can fill on nice weekends because of the nearby bike trails.
ma_main_crag.parking_note: A small dirt lot on College Street serves the park; it also serves the bike trails, so it fills on pleasant weekends.
ma_main_crag.approach: From the lot, stroll south along the dirt track for 50 to 100 yards, then cut east into the trees to reach the rock.
